sections.h: Atrahasis: humans made to carry the gods' basket
sections.b: The Babylonian poem Atrahasis begins "When the gods were man": junior gods dig the rivers and carry the work basket until they strike (Atrahasis 1:1-2:151). The great gods solve the crisis by making humans: "let man carry the god's work basket" (Atrahasis 3:10). A. R. Millard saw that Genesis shares the idea of humans set to work (Genesis 2:15), but in Genesis the garden already grows, God is not tired, and hard toil comes only after sin (Genesis 3:17-19). Work in Genesis is a calling under a God who rests and gives rest (Genesis 2:2-3; Mark 2:27).
sections.refs: Atrahasis 1:1-44; Atrahasis 3:10; Genesis 2:15; Genesis 3:17-19; Genesis 2:2-3; Mark 2:27

common: Many ancient peoples said humans were made to serve the gods by working for them.

claude.title: Basket and garden
claude.body: My reading: the work basket of Atrahasis and the garden of Genesis 2 are two answers to one question. In the poem, work is a burden the gods escape by passing it down; in Genesis, it is a trust given by a God who keeps working (John 5:17) and who later takes the yoke on himself to give rest (Matthew 11:28-30).

sections.h: The council of the gods in Atrahasis
sections.b: In Atrahasis the high gods draw lots for heaven, earth and the deep waters (Atrahasis 1:11-16), then meet as a court when the junior gods revolt (Atrahasis 2:63-74). They argue, fear one another, and settle the matter by vote (Atrahasis 3:43-45). The Bible's pictures of a heavenly council (1 Kings 22:19-20; Psalm 82:1; Job 1:6) differ at the root: the LORD sits on the throne, the members are his creatures, and he judges them (Psalm 82:6-7).
sections.refs: Atrahasis 1:11-16; Atrahasis 2:63-74; Atrahasis 3:43-45; 1 Kings 22:19-20; Psalm 82:1-7; Job 1:6

sections.h: The Igigi's revolt and the Watchers
sections.b: The Babylonian Atrahasis tells of junior gods, the Igigi, who burn their tools and besiege Enlil's house because their labor is too heavy (Atrahasis 2:1-2:151). Helge Kvanvig compared this with the Watchers of 1 Enoch: in Atrahasis the revolt leads to humans made to toil; in the Watchers story, to giants for whom humans must toil. The differences are large: the Igigi are vindicated and never punished, while the Watchers sin through lust and forbidden teaching and are bound for judgment (1 Enoch 10:4-12; Jude 1:6; 2 Peter 2:4). The site's verdict: the same beings, unlikely; a shared motif of revolt in heaven before the Flood, real.
sections.refs: Atrahasis 2:1-151; 1 Enoch 6:1-6; 1 Enoch 10:4-12; Jude 1:6; 2 Peter 2:4; Genesis 6:1-4

uncommon: Some readers see the Igigi's revolt in Atrahasis as a distorted memory of the angels' rebellion.

sections.h: Gods who sleep, weep and fear
sections.b: Atrahasis shows the gods of Babylon asleep while their house is surrounded (Atrahasis 2:42-43), pale with fear (Atrahasis 2:57) and in tears (Atrahasis 2:143). Elijah mocked Baal in the same terms: "maybe he's asleep" (1 Kings 18:27), and Israel sang that its God "does not doze and does not sleep" (Psalm 121:4). Christian readers take two lines from Scripture on such gods: they are "nothing" (1 Corinthians 8:4; Psalm 96:5), and what is offered to them goes to demons (1 Corinthians 10:20; Deuteronomy 32:17). Justin Martyr and Augustine read the pagan gods as fallen spirits.

sections.h: Atrahasis: humans from clay, blood and spittle
sections.b: In Atrahasis one god, We-ila, is slaughtered, and the birth goddess mixes his flesh and blood with clay; the junior gods spit on it, and fourteen lumps become seven males and seven females (Atrahasis 3:33-3:104). Genesis shares the clay and the divine potter (Genesis 2:7; Isaiah 64:8; Job 33:6) but not the slain god. Millard noted that "no hint of the use of dead deity" is found in Genesis, and that the gods' spitting is "very different" from God breathing the breath of life. Gerhard Hasel argued that Genesis 1 deliberately answers the Mesopotamian picture of humans made to feed the gods.

sections.h: Image of God, or replacement for the gods?
sections.b: The Babylonian Atrahasis makes humans to take over the gods' labor: "let man carry the god's work basket" (Atrahasis 3:10). Genesis makes them "in our image, as our likeness" to rule (Genesis 1:26-28), and blesses them. Gerhard Hasel read Genesis 1 as a conscious reply: man is not "an afterthought" to supply the gods' needs; God supplies his. Both texts give humans something divine in them, a slain god's flesh and ghost in the poem, God's image and breath in Genesis (Genesis 1:27; Genesis 2:7).

sections.h: A god's blood in the clay
sections.b: In Atrahasis humans are made from clay mixed with the flesh and blood of a slaughtered god (Atrahasis 3:33-3:53). The Bible also ties life to blood (Leviticus 17:11; Genesis 9:4-6), but it never makes humans from a dead god. The New Testament speaks of divine blood in another way: God's church "which he acquired through his own blood" (Acts 20:28), given freely to set people free (Hebrews 9:14).

sections.h: Forced labor in Atrahasis and Exodus
sections.b: The junior gods of Atrahasis cry that "the work basket has been killing us" (Atrahasis 2:125), and their cry is answered by making humans to carry it instead; the goddess even calls the change a "release" (andurāru, Atrahasis 3:78), the word Babylonian kings used for freeing debt-slaves. Israel's cry under forced labor in Egypt is answered the other way: "I have heard their outcry" (Exodus 3:7), and the LORD frees them, breaks the yoke (Leviticus 26:13) and commands a release for all (Leviticus 25:10; Luke 4:18).
sections.refs: Atrahasis 2:125; Atrahasis 3:78; Exodus 1:13-14; Exodus 3:7; Leviticus 26:13; Leviticus 25:10; Luke 4:18

sections.b: Atrahasis sets a purifying rite "on the first, the seventh and the fifteenth day of the month" (Atrahasis 3:31). The fifteenth is šapattu, a word that sounds like Hebrew shabbat. A. R. Millard answered those who link them: the Akkadian word "denotes specifically the full moon ... on the fifteenth day of the lunar month," and "no derived Sabbath existed in Babylonia." The Sabbath counts sevens of days from creation (Genesis 2:2-3; Exodus 20:9-10), not phases of the moon.
